name: Confessor Ivo Marrant
appearance: A Confessor in his forties in the grey cloak of his order, who puts his hood back in the cold so that his bald head is bare to the snow: a pleasant, well-fed face, round and clean-shaven, the cheeks pink with cold, pale brows that hardly show, small light-grey eyes that hold very still, a small mark on the chin, and a smile of neat, even teeth that he gives to a whole court at once. He carries the iron censer on its chain in his own hand, so that he stands in his own grey weather, and the smell of hot iron reaches a gate ahead of his voice. At the bars he held nothing but the censer and the writ. His grey cloak fastens at the throat with a plain iron toggle.
portrait_alt: Portrait of Confessor Ivo Marrant: a bald, round-faced, clean-shaven man in his forties, snow settling on his bare scalp, pink-cheeked, with small light-grey eyes and a pleasant close-lipped smile showing neat teeth, in a heavy grey wool cloak with its hood pushed back, fastened with an iron toggle, holding an iron chain in one hand while thin grey smoke curls up beside him, before dark iron gate bars and a stone wall in falling snow.
last_seen_doing: Going down the first flight of the Steps into the dusk after the Captain of the Ninth gave his name at the bars; he had looked at Darrow's face, called him Captain, and thanked the Prior for her candour.
now: Camped on the lower terrace below the gate of Saint Ysolde's with four grey cloaks; the sixth of them keeps the winch-house. He read his list at the bars and was answered by Old Mercy and the law of names. Then the Captain of the Ninth crossed the court and gave his name at the bars; Marrant looked at his face, called him Captain, and thanked the Prior for her candour. He has said he will wait. That night his camp sat up in turns round one fire, where the whole House could see it, and a man of his at the bars sent the Captain of the Ninth the Confessor's good night, by his rank.
story_so_far: He led the grey cloaks up the Holloway and the Thousand Steps and came to the gate of Saint Ysolde's in the hour before dusk, five at the bars and the sixth at the winch-house, with the censer in his own hand. He had been told at the winch-house fire that the Faithless had gone down the far side a week since, and read his list anyway: he has read to empty beds before, he said, and finds it steadies the hand. He held his paper out for the wicket under the law of guests until the Prior could not refuse it without breaking that law; when the wicket opened a hand's width, two of his men came through, and Old Mercy rang late and stopped them a pace from the wounded. Mother Ione gave him the law's other half: no name under the bell is taken down against its will. He called her bell fine and a little slow on the rope, made his camp on the lower terrace, and called for the Captain of the Ninth to come down and kneel. The Captain came to the bars instead and gave his name; Marrant called him Captain and thanked the Prior for her candour.

known_facts.fact: He came to the bars with four grey cloaks in the hour before dusk; the sixth of them had stayed at the winch-house with his boots on Rae Thorne's cart.
He named himself to the Prior as Ivo Marrant, Confessor, under the Knight-Confessor's seal, as if they had corresponded.

He had been told at the winch-house fire that the Faithless of Harrow Ford went down the far side a week since, and read anyway: he has read to empty beds before, he said, and finds it steadies the hand.
known_facts.evidence: I find it steadies the hand.

known_facts.fact: He unrolled the writ against the bars so the court could see its seal, blue wax the size of a child's palm, and read Darrow's name first and Hollis's second, then the Ninth's names and the Sixth's, slow, so the court could count.
known_facts.evidence: slow, so the court could count

known_facts.fact: He did not read the far cots, and said so himself: the Crown has no quarrel with men who can't answer.
known_facts.evidence: The Crown has no quarrel with men who can't answer.

known_facts.fact: He held the writ out for the wicket under the law of guests, as a courier's paper, and when the Prior made him wait he said he would hate to tell the bell-houses her House broke one old law to keep a courier standing in the cold; when the wicket opened a hand's width, two of his men came through it and a third held it open.
known_facts.evidence: I'd hate to tell the bell-houses

known_facts.fact: What Darrow read in him at the bars: a fire, all of it poured, and under the pouring nothing of his own; no lie in him, and the wicket already open in his mind.
known_facts.evidence: nothing of his own at all

known_facts.fact: When Old Mercy rang and the Prior spoke the law of names, his eyes went past her shoulder to Maelis and stayed there a beat longer than courtesy, and his smile changed its weight.

He told the Prior she keeps a fine bell, a little slow on the rope, called his two men back out through the wicket, and said the grey below the gate where the springs steam is the law's ground and nobody's: they would make their fire on the lower terrace, and bells grow tired.
known_facts.evidence: A little slow on the rope.

known_facts.fact: He called for Ser Darrow by name to the whole court, as a man says a name he is sure of: come down and kneel, and the rest of the paper goes back into his cloak and never comes out; he would wait, it is the thing he is best at.
known_facts.evidence: It's the thing I'm best at.

known_facts.fact: Called back from the head of the Steps by both his names, he came to the bars and looked at the Captain's face, the first time anyone in grey had; told that he had read to a full bed, he paused the length of a man deciding to be pleased, called him Captain, and thanked the Prior for her candour.
known_facts.evidence: Mother Ione. Thank you for your candour.

known_facts.fact: On the night he camped below the gate, one of his men at the bars asked the gate-ward, very civil, to give the Captain of the Ninth the Confessor's good night, by his rank.
known_facts.evidence: to give the Captain of the Ninth the Confessor's good night

known_facts.fact: When the lay brothers carried the feast bread down, he thanked the House for its charity and gave them his name for Benedek's Hollowing to carry back up: ember witchcraft.

relationships.label: the Prior who answered his writ with the bell
relationships.note: She made him wait at the wicket for the bell, answered his men with the bell and the law of names, and was thanked for her candour when the Captain gave his name at her gate.

relationships.label: the first name on his paper, who answered to it
relationships.note: He read Darrow's name first at the bars without knowing his face; then Darrow crossed the court and gave his name and rank through the bars, and Marrant looked at his face and called him Captain.

relationships.label: the Mender at the Prior's shoulder
relationships.note: When the bell was rung his eyes went to her and stayed a beat longer than courtesy, and she gave him nothing back.
